questions.q: Inside a normal method, when is the value of this decided?
questions.explain: this is not fixed in the code. For milk.describe() it is milk; for ada.describe() it is ada, even if both share one function.
options: Each time the function is called, by what stands before the dot
When the object is created with { }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both objects hold the same function, so the comparison is true. When called as ada.describe(), this is ada.

questions.q: Why does ["Fix sink"].map(list.label) lose this?
questions.explain: Writing list.label without calling it takes the function off its object. When map calls it later, there is no list. in front, so this is undefined.
options: map receives only the function, not the object it came from, and calls it without a dot
Strings cannot be passed to methods

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: greet("Grace") has no dot, so this is undefined (class code is always strict). Reading this.name from undefined throws a TypeError.
options:
Ada greets Grace
Ada greets Grace

Ada greets Grace
undefined greets Grace

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The arrow function calls list.label(task) with a dot, so this is list. Wrapping a method in an arrow is one of the two standard fixes.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'name')

questions.q: What does list.label.bind(list) return?
questions.explain: bind does not call anything. It makes a new function that always runs with this set to list, so you can pass it as a callback safely.
options: A new function whose this is fixed to list forever

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The bound function always uses counter as this, even when called without a dot. It runs three times, so count is 3.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'count')

questions.q: Inside a method labelAll() { return this.tasks.map((task) => this.label(task)); }, why does this work in the arrow function?
questions.explain: An arrow takes this from the code around it. Here that is labelAll, called as list.labelAll(), so this is list. That is why arrows make great callbacks inside methods.
options: Arrow functions have no this of their own; they use the this of labelAll
Arrow functions always use the global object as this
It does not work; it throws a TypeError

questions.q: Why is label: () => this.name a bad way to write a method on an object?
questions.explain: Arrows have no this of their own, so this comes from where the object is written (the module, where it is undefined). Use the short method form label() { } for methods and arrows for callbacks.
options: The arrow takes this from the surrounding module, not from the object
It is too slow for methods

questions.q: Which is not one of the things new Task("Buy milk") does?
questions.explain: new creates an object, links it to the prototype, calls the constructor and returns the object. Methods are not copied: they live once on the prototype and are shared.
options: Calls Task with this set to the new object
Copies every method of Task.prototype into the new object

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: complete lives once on Task.prototype, so it is not an own key of milk. Both tasks share that one function, so the comparison is true.

questions.q: You read milk.toString, but milk has no own toString. What does JavaScript do?
questions.explain: This path is the prototype chain. toString is found at the end of it, on Object.prototype, which every ordinary object shares.
options: Looks at milk's prototype, then that prototype's prototype, until it finds it or reaches null
Searches every object in the program

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: title is the object's own property. complete is inherited: Object.hasOwn says no, but in follows the prototype chain and says yes.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A class is still a function with a prototype underneath. Methods written in the class go on the prototype, so only title is an own key.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: complete returns this, the task itself, so you can call another method straight after it. The task is done, so it shows [x].
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'describe')

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Classes add a safety rule: calling one without new throws a TypeError. An old constructor function would quietly run with the wrong this.

questions.q: What does milk instanceof Task check?
questions.explain: instanceof walks the prototype chain. That is why a RecurringTask is also instanceof Task: Task.prototype is further up its chain.
options: Whether milk was created in the same file as Task
Whether Task.prototype is somewhere on milk's prototype chain
Whether milk has the same keys as a Task

questions.q: A class has a private field #id. What happens if code outside the class writes task.#id?
questions.explain: Only code inside the class may use # names. JavaScript checks this before running, so the whole file fails with a SyntaxError.
options: It works, but prints a warning
It is a SyntaxError: the program does not even start
It creates a new public property called #id

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Private fields are hidden from Object.keys, and the getter lives on the prototype. Reading acc.balance runs the getter, which returns the private value.

questions.q: A class has a getter id but no setter. What does this print?
questions.explain: Without a setter, the property is read-only. Class code is strict, so assigning to it throws a TypeError, and the value stays 7.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The constructor's this.title = title goes through the setter, so the spaces are trimmed. The setter then refuses the empty title and the old one stays.
options:
Rejected: title must not be empty
[Buy milk]

Rejected: title must not be empty
[  Buy milk ]

Rejected: title must not be empty
[]

questions.q: What is a setter like set title(value) { … } the right place for?
questions.explain: A setter runs every time someone assigns the property. It can clean and check the value and refuse bad input, just like the lesson's title setter refuses empty text.
options: Storing the value in a global variable
Checking the new value, so no outside code can put the object into a bad state
Making the property invisible to getters
Creating new objects of the class

questions.q: How do you call a static method fromJSON of class Task?
questions.explain: A static member belongs to the class itself, not to each object. It is often used as another way to create objects, like Task.fromJSON(text).

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: static #nextId is one counter shared by the whole class, not one per task. Each constructor takes the current value and adds 1. Nobody outside can reset it.

questions.q: In a class that extends Task, what must its constructor do before using this?
questions.explain: In a derived class, this does not exist until super() has run. Using this before it throws a ReferenceError.
options: Call super(...), which runs the parent's constructor

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: this.extra = true runs before super(title). In a derived class, this does not exist yet, so JavaScript throws a ReferenceError.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: describe overrides the parent's version and reuses it through super.describe(). Task.prototype is on the chain, so the object is an instance of both classes.
options:
[ ] Take out bins (every 7 days)
true true

[ ] Take out bins (every 7 days)
true false

questions.q: The lesson's TaskList has a method written #find(id). What does the # mean?
questions.explain: Like private fields, private methods start with #. Outside code cannot call list.#find(1), so the class decides how tasks are looked up.
options: The method runs automatically when the class is created
It is a private method: only code inside the class can call it

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: forEach(list.add) passes the method without its object, so this is undefined and reading #tasks throws. Only the two arrow calls and the last call added tasks, so the count is 3.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: openCount is a getter, so you read it like a property, without (). Three tasks, one completed, so 2 are open.

questions.q: You have LoggingTaskList extends TaskList and AuditedTaskList extends TaskList. Now someone needs both features. What is the problem with inheritance here?
questions.explain: Inheritance fixes one combination per class. With composition, one TaskList takes helpers (listeners) and covers every combination.
options: JavaScript cannot extend a class twice in one file
You need yet another class for the combination, and every new feature doubles the number of classes
Private fields cannot be inherited at all

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first list has no listeners, so nothing is recorded. Each list has its own private #tasks, so the watched list's ids start at 1.

questions.q: Which is a good use of inheritance (extends), following the lesson's rule of thumb?
questions.explain: Use inheritance for a true, stable "is a" relationship. "Has a" or "uses a" (a logger, a database, an e-mail sender) is composition: pass the helper in.
options: A service that uses a database
RecurringTask extends Task: a recurring task truly is a task

questions.q: Passing helpers into a class through its constructor, like new TaskList({ listeners: [log] }), is called what?
questions.explain: The class receives the things it depends on instead of creating them itself. ZudoJS is built on this: @zudojs/container creates your classes and hands each one its helpers.

questions.q: Finish the Task class. priority is a getter and setter backed by a private field #priority with default 3. The setter accepts only whole numbers from 1 to 5 and throws new Error("bad priority") otherwise. The program should print 3, 1, bad priority, 1, each on its own line.
questions.explain: The private field holds the value; the getter returns it; the setter checks with Number.isInteger and the range before saving. A refused value leaves the old priority in place.

questions.q: Write DeadlineTask extends Task. Its constructor takes title and due. Override describe() so it adds , due <date> after the parent's text. Use super in both places. The program should print [ ] File taxes, due 2026-10-01.
questions.explain: super(title) must run before this.due = due. super.describe() reuses the parent's text instead of rewriting it.

questions.q: The last line loses this and crashes. Fix only that line (with an arrow function or bind) so all three items are added. The program should print 3.
questions.explain: forEach(cart.add) passes the method without its object. (item) => cart.add(item) calls it with a dot again; cart.add.bind(cart) works too.

questions.q: Add a static method fromJSON(text) to Task. It parses the JSON text, creates a task with the title, and sets done to true only when the data's done is exactly true. The program should print Write report true false.
questions.explain: A static method is called on the class. data.done === true makes sure that text like "yes" does not count as done.

questions.q: Finish Account: a private #balance starting at 0, a deposit(amount) method that throws new Error("amount must be positive") when amount is not above 0, and a balance getter. The program should print 50, amount must be positive, 50.
questions.explain: The balance is private, so the only way to change it is deposit, which checks the amount first. Without a setter, nobody can write acc.balance = 1000000.

questions.q: Finish TaskList using composition: store the listeners array passed to the constructor, and in add(title) call every listener with title. The program should print log: Buy milk and then [ 'Buy milk' ].
questions.explain: The list does not know what the helpers do; it just calls them. Adding a feature means passing one more function, not writing a new subclass.

questions.q: Add a complete method to Task.prototype (the old constructor-function style) that sets this.done to true. The program should print true false true.
questions.explain: Use a normal function, not an arrow, so this is the task before the dot. The method lives once on the prototype and all tasks share it.

questions.q: Write Square extends Rect. Its constructor takes one side and calls the parent constructor with it as both width and height. Override describe() to return "square " + super.describe(). The program should print square 3x3 = 9.
questions.explain: super(side, side) runs Rect's constructor with both sizes. super.describe() calls the parent's version, and the child adds its word in front.

questions.q: Finish the Query class so its methods can be chained. where(text) adds text to the private #parts array and returns the object itself; build() returns the parts joined with " AND ". The program should print done = true AND owner = ada.
questions.explain: Returning this from where gives back the same object, so the next method can be called straight after it, like complete() in the lesson.

questions.q: A Logger method is passed to forEach as a callback. Create write with bind so that this stays the logger. The program should print [api] started and [api] ready.
questions.explain: logger.write alone is just the function, so this is lost. logger.write.bind(logger) returns a function whose this is always logger.
